claims.text: An integrated model incorporating atomic-scale disorder, multiphase microstructure, and interstitial effects will identify low-phonon-conductivity high-entropy alloys more accurately than current continuum or empirical models.
The initial material is equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr.
HfNbTaTiZr can be synthesized using sintering followed by controlled cooling.
Slow cooling produces a multiphase beta-BCC plus alpha-HCP HfNbTaTiZr structure.
Water quenching produces a metastable single-phase beta-BCC HfNbTaTiZr structure.
The processed HfNbTaTiZr alloy contains approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
The proposed predictive approach integrates lattice distortion, phase-boundary scattering, and interstitial-atom effects.
Controlled thermal processing can ensure reproducible phase formation and oxygen content.
Compositional complexity and interstitial oxygen induce lattice distortions.
Lattice distortions and multiphase microstructural features act as phonon scatterers.
Atomic-scale disorder and multiphase interfaces enhance phonon scattering.
Enhanced phonon scattering reduces phonon mean free paths and consequently lowers phonon thermal conductivity.
Traditional models based on averaged lattice properties miss local disruption effects from disorder and phase interfaces.
The model will identify alloys whose predicted phonon thermal conductivities are at least 20–25% lower than values predicted by conventional empirical methods.
The model's advantage will be greatest for alloys having high lattice distortion and well-defined multiphase structures.
The approach is mainly applicable to high-entropy alloys with compositional complexity and phase behavior similar to equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr and may not apply to simpler or minimally disordered alloys.
Experimental comparison of model forecasts with measured phonon thermal conductivities in multiphase and single-phase HfNbTaTiZr samples can test the hypothesis.

The hypothesis is falsified if the new approach achieves less than a 20% improvement in correlation with measured conductivity relative to conventional models or fails to capture the trend between multiphase and single-phase samples.
